title: Epistola Ad Augustinum
author: Prosperus Aquitanus

passages.original: Unde sequatur gratiam secundum merita hominum dari, et proinde gratiam jam non esse gratiam. Hunc vero filiorum tenebrarum versutiam et Orientalium episcoporum judicio, et sedis apostolicæ auctoritate, et Africanorum præsulum vigilantia fuisse manifestatam. S. Augustinum, quem dicit S. Prosper tunc fuisse præcipuam portionem Domini sacerdotum, hanc scriptis libris polemicis destruxisse, talemque hæresim omni ex parte debellasse ; quosdam tamen inter catholicos in Galliis inveniri, qui doctrinam ejus librasque malignis rumoribus infamarent, diventes eum liberum arbitrium penitus submovere, et sub nomine gratiæ necessitatem prædicare fatalem, duas etiam ab ipso credivelle uno in homine naturas.
passages.english: From this it would follow that grace is given according to human merits, and that grace is therefore no longer grace. But this cunning of the sons of darkness, [he says,] had been exposed by the judgment of the Eastern bishops, by the authority of the apostolic see, and by the vigilance of the African prelates. Saint Augustine, whom Saint Prosper says was at that time the chief portion of the Lord's priests, had destroyed it in the polemical books he wrote, and had defeated such a heresy on every side; yet some were found among the Catholics in Gaul who defamed his teaching and his books with malicious rumours, saying that he did away with free will altogether, and under the name of grace preached fatal necessity, and also that he believed there were two natures in one man.
passages.notes: Read 'librosque' for 'librasque', 'dicentes' for 'diventes', and 'credidisse' (or similar) for the corrupt 'credivelle'. 'Hunc ... versutiam' is ungrammatical (for 'hanc'); translated as 'this cunning'. The passage is a summary in reported speech of Prosper's letter.

passages.original: quæ tum creata esset recta, a rectitudine primi hominis peccato decidit, mortique æternæ facta est obnoxia : sed nova in Christo creatione reparandam, qui libertatem hominis reparando et continuis auxiliis præveniendo salvat. Operi finem imponit (Num. 20), Rufinum amicum exhortando ut Augustini disputationibus cognoscendis curam impendat, si vere de sana circa Dei gratiam doctrina instrui desideret sicut eum desiderare conveniebat.
passages.english: [one nature,] which, though it was created upright, fell from uprightness through the sin of the first man and became liable to eternal death, but is to be restored by the new creation in Christ, who saves by restoring man's freedom and going before it with continual aids. He brings the work to an end (no. 20) by urging his friend Rufinus to take care to become acquainted with Augustine's arguments, if he truly wishes to be instructed in sound doctrine concerning the grace of God, as it was fitting that he should wish.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing 'one nature altogether' from the preceding context. 'Num.' is taken as a section number of the letter.
